content.text: Accuracy weights each class by its size, so when one class is rare it mostly measures the common one. A rule that always predicts the majority can score 99% and catch nothing. Compare every model with that baseline, read the four counts of the confusion matrix, and summarize with a metric that gives each class its own weight.

A quality team wants a model that flags defective parts on an assembly line, where about 1 part in 100 is bad. Three candidates reach the review with an accuracy of 0.990, 0.990 and 0.976. The third one is dropped first. It's also the only one that catches the defects: 48 of the 50 in the test set. One of the two "best" candidates is a rule that calls every part fine.
The common misconception
Many developers read accuracy as a universal grade: higher is better and 99% is excellent, whatever the data looks like. It's easy to see why:

items.text: on every scikit-learn classifier returns accuracy, and it's the first number most tutorials print.
It's intuitive: the share of predictions that were right. Nobody needs a definition.
On balanced data it does its job. Google's Machine Learning Crash Course calls it a coarse-grained measure of model quality when both classes have similar numbers of examples.

content.text: The half-truth: accuracy is exact about what it measures. When one class is rare, what it measures stops being what you care about.
What actually happens
Accuracy is the number of correct predictions, true positives plus true negatives, divided by all predictions. That formula hides a weighting.
Accuracy is an average weighted by class size
Split accuracy by class and it becomes the hit rate on positives times their share of the data, plus the hit rate on negatives times theirs. With
class imbalance

at 1% positives, 99% of the weight sits on the negatives. A model that finds 14 of 50 defects has a hit rate of 0.28 on them, which adds 0.0028 to its accuracy. Catching every single defect could add at most one point.
The floor isn't zero
DummyClassifier
makes predictions that ignore the input features, and scikit-learn presents it as a simple
baseline

to compare against. Its default strategy always predicts the most frequent class, so it scores exactly the majority's share: 0.990 on this data. The useful range for accuracy here runs from 0.990 to 1.000, not from 0 to 1. scikit-learn's guide adds that when a classifier's accuracy is too close to random, something probably went wrong, and lists class imbalance among the usual suspects.

The floor moves with the data. The same always-negative rule scores 0.5 on a balanced test set, 0.99 here and 0.999 when positives are 1 in 1,000. Accuracy describes the test set's class mix as much as the model.
Count the four outcomes
Here are the three candidates from the review: the dummy rule, a logistic regression (model A), and the same model trained with
class_weight="balanced"
so that missing a rare positive costs more (model B).

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20_000, n_features=10, n_informative=4,
                           weights=[0.99], flip_y=0, class_sep=2.0,
                           random_state=1)  # 1% positive
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)
models = {
    "always negative": DummyClassifier(),
    "model A": LogisticRegression(),
    "model B": LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced"),
}
for name, model in models.items():
    accuracy = model.fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te)
    print(f"{name:<15} accuracy {accuracy:.3f}")
# always negative accuracy 0.990
# model A         accuracy 0.990
# model B         accuracy 0.976
# "Model B is the worst of the three"

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score, confusion_matrix
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20_000, n_features=10, n_informative=4,
                           weights=[0.99], flip_y=0, class_sep=2.0,
                           random_state=1)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y, random_state=0)
models = {
    "always negative": DummyClassifier(),
    "model A": LogisticRegression(),
    "model B": LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced"),
}
for name, model in models.items():
    pred = model.fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict(X_te)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_te, pred).ravel()
    bal = balanced_accuracy_score(y_te, pred)
    print(f"{name:<15} TP {tp:>2}  FN {fn:>2}  FP {fp:>3}  balanced {bal:.3f}")
# always negative TP  0  FN 50  FP   0  balanced 0.500
# model A         TP 14  FN 36  FP  15  balanced 0.638
# model B         TP 48  FN  2  FP 117  balanced 0.968

content.text: The
confusion matrix

splits predictions into four counts: true positives (defects caught), false negatives (defects missed), false positives (false alarms) and true negatives. In scikit-learn, rows are the true classes and columns the predicted ones. Now the models separate. Model A misses 36 of the 50 defects and still ties the dummy on accuracy, because 0.990 rewards the 4,950 good parts far more than the 50 bad ones. Model B catches 48 and pays with 117 false alarms. Accuracy merged all of that into one number and ranked the only useful model last.
One number that respects both classes
Balanced accuracy

averages the recall of each class, the share of each class the model got right, so the 50 defects weigh as much as the 4,950 good parts. scikit-learn's guide gives its two key properties: on balanced data it equals ordinary accuracy, and when accuracy beats chance only by exploiting the imbalance, it drops to 1 divided by the number of classes, 0.5 here. The dummy gets exactly 0.500, model A 0.638 and model B 0.968. The ranking finally matches what the models do. With
adjusted=True
, random guessing scores 0 instead.

rows.text: Always predicting "fine" scores 0.990 here, with no model at all
Higher accuracy means a better model
Model B catches 48 of 50 defects and has the lowest accuracy, 0.976
A model that beats 0.99 has learned something
Model A missed 36 of 50 defects and tied the dummy
It also describes the class mix: the same rule scores 0.5 or 0.99

blocks.title: Get the floor and the per-class view in one call

content.text: Put
DummyClassifier
in the same loop as your real models, so the baseline is printed next to every score. Then call
classification_report(y_te, pred)
: it prints precision, recall and F1 for each class, which shows a weak minority class at a glance.

blocks.title: Don't balance the test set to rescue accuracy

content.text: Undersampling the test set to 50/50 makes accuracy readable, but it changes the world you're testing in. Model B's false-alarm rate is about 2.4%: on 4,950 good parts that's 117 alarms, on 50 it would be one or two. Its flags would look almost always right, then drown the team in false alarms in production. Keep the real class mix in the test set and change the metric instead.

blocks.title: Balanced accuracy has a blind spot

content.text: It's built from recall alone, so it never looks at how many flags are wrong. Of model B's 165 flags, 117 are false alarms: only 29% of what it flags is a real defect. Whether that's acceptable depends on what each mistake costs, the subject of the next article in this path.
How to apply it in your project
Print the share of each class, for example with
value_counts(normalize=True)
in pandas. If one class dominates, accuracy alone is out.

items.title: Put a dummy in every comparison

content.text: DummyClassifier
gives the floor. A model is only as good as its distance above it.
Use
confusion_matrix
or
classification_report
before any single number, and look at the minority class row.

items.title: Pick the summary for the question

content.text: Balanced accuracy for one fair number, recall when misses are expensive, precision when false alarms are. The Crash Course gives the same guidance for recall and precision.
Split with
stratify=y
so training and test sets keep the class proportions you'll see in production.
Key takeaways

items.text: Accuracy weights each class by its size; with 1% positives, the positives barely move it.
The floor is the majority's share, not zero: always predicting "fine" scored 0.990, the same as a model that missed 36 of 50 defects.
Read the confusion matrix: accuracy ranked the only model that caught 48 of 50 defects last.
Balanced accuracy gives each class equal weight, but it ignores false alarms, so check precision too.
